opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we debated a lot internally. The honest answer is that we started from the customer, not from the infrastructure. When we talked to developers building with AI agents, what they needed wasn't another index to query. They needed a way to hand off a hard research task and get back something accurate, well-sourced, and structured enough that their own systems could act on it. That's an agent-shaped problem, not an index-shaped problem.

There's also a sequencing argument. Building a web-scale index is an enormous, capital-intensive undertaking, and if you build it in a vacuum, you end up optimizing for the wrong things. You'd probably copy the assumptions of the human web, ranking for clicks, for a person scanning ten blue links. But the agents using our product aren't people. They read everything, they care about tokens and latency and verifiability, and they want evidence they can reason over. We wanted to learn what that consumer needs before committing to an index design.

So launching with the agent first gave us a tight feedback loop. Every task tells us where retrieval fell short: which sources were missing, where freshness mattered, where we needed deeper coverage of a domain. That signal shapes how we build the index underneath. In a way, the agent is how we discover what the index should be.

And frankly, it let us deliver value quickly. Customers don't buy an index; they buy outcomes. If we can get them high-quality answers on hard questions today, we earn the right, and the data and conviction, to go build the deeper infrastructure. Over time, the index and the agents co-evolve, and I think that's how you end up building something that's actually designed for the web's second user, which is AI.

r002.rationale: It describes building an index as capital-intensive and warns against designing it in a vacuum, but does not characterize an index as a latency optimization.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts agent-shaped needs with human search assumptions, but does not state that competing with human search users was easier than competing directly with a search engine.

r004.rationale: It says agent tasks provide feedback on retrieval gaps that shapes the index, and that the agent helps discover what the index should be as both co-evolve—communicating incremental index development.

fable-5.1.text:
So, first off, I'd push back a little on the premise. We didn't launch with an agent and then decide to build an index later. We actually started from the belief that the index was the thing that mattered, and the agent was how we learned what the index needed to be.

Here's the way I think about it. When you're building infrastructure for AI, the customer isn't a person typing ten blue links worth of queries. The customer is a model. And a model asks very different questions than a human does. It asks longer questions. It asks compound questions. It cares about different things, like whether a fact is current, or whether a source can be trusted, or whether two pieces of information from different pages actually agree with each other. Nobody had a good map of what that demand looked like, because the whole category was new.

So if we had gone and spent eighteen months and a lot of capital building a web-scale index first, we would have been building it against our guesses about what agents want. And I've been through enough of those cycles at Twitter to know that your guesses about usage are usually wrong in ways you can't predict from the whiteboard.

The agent let us put something in front of real developers very early. Every query that came through it taught us something. We could see where the existing retrieval sources fell short, where latency mattered versus where depth mattered, which kinds of pages were being hit over and over, and which parts of the web nobody actually needed for this use case. That's an incredibly valuable signal, and you only get it by shipping.

There's also a practical point, which is that you can get surprisingly far by orchestrating across what already exists while you build your own foundation underneath it. The agent layer isn't a stopgap. It's the thing the index ultimately has to serve. So we started where the learning was fastest, and let the harder, more expensive layer be shaped by evidence instead of by intuition.

r002.rationale: It describes the index as important infrastructure shaped by evidence, not as a latency optimization.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the difficulty of competing with human search users to competing directly with a search engine.

r004.rationale: It says the agent exposed real developer queries and taught the team what the index needed, so they could build the foundation incrementally based on evidence.

astra-6.text:
We started with a search agent because we wanted to understand what useful search looks like when the user is an AI. It’s not necessarily a list of links. The agent is trying to accomplish a task, and it needs information it can reason over and trust.

Building that layer first lets you work backward from the task: What information is missing? Where does existing search work well, and where does it fall short? That gives you a much clearer idea of what you need from an index. An index is a substantial investment, and we wanted the requirements to come from the needs of the agents we were serving.

sol-6.1.text:
We started with the search agent because we wanted to understand what an AI actually needs from the web. A traditional search engine is built to give a person links to click. An agent needs to find information, evaluate it, and bring back evidence that helps it complete a task.

Building that layer first let us learn where existing search worked and where it fell short. That gives us a much clearer idea of what to build underneath it. A full index is a substantial investment, and we wanted that investment to be guided by the needs of the agents using it.
